title: Section check: People, memory and shared histories
intro: 6 questions about Lessons 10–12. Take your time. You can look back at the lessons and try again as often as you like.

questions.question: The photo of the covered bridge in Hội An was taken in 2018. What kind of evidence is it?

options.text: A picture of the port in the 1400s
options.feedback: Not quite. The photo was taken in 2018, hundreds of years after the port began. Look back at Lesson 10.

options.text: A view of a place that is still there
options.feedback: Yes. The photo shows the bridge on one day in 2018. It cannot show the old traders.

options.text: A record written by an early trader
options.feedback: Not quite. It is a photo, not a written record. And it was taken in 2018. Look back at Lesson 10.

questions.question: UNESCO describes Hội An's shops, homes and quay. What else could help you learn how people saw the town long ago?

options.text: Old records or objects from that time
options.feedback: Yes. Buildings show us a place. Old records and objects could help us hear the views of people who lived there.

options.text: A newer photo of the covered bridge
options.feedback: Not quite. A new photo shows the bridge today. It cannot show what people thought long ago. Look back at Lesson 10.

options.text: A longer list of the town's buildings
options.feedback: Not quite. Buildings tell us about the place, not what each person thought. Look back at Lesson 10.

questions.question: Which question can the 1976 photo of Borobudur help you answer?

options.text: What did the first builders plan?
options.feedback: Not quite. Borobudur was built in the 700s and 800s. A photo from 1976 cannot show the builders' plans. Look back at Lesson 11.

options.text: Why did the team choose each repair?
options.feedback: Not quite. A photo shows the work, not the reasons for it. Written records or a worker's memories could help. Look back at Lesson 11.

options.text: What did the repairs look like?
options.feedback: Yes. The photo records one moment of modern conservation work, in 1976.

questions.question: The Borobudur team kept its photos, drawings and notes. People can study them later. What is a set of records like this called?

options.feedback: Not quite. A stupa is a bell-shaped tower on the monument. Look back at Lesson 11.
Yes. An archive keeps records safe. Later, people can compare them and ask why each repair was made.
Not quite. Recognition is when a group says something is important. In 2017, UNESCO said this about the archive. Look back at Lesson 11.

stimulus.title: A made-up class exhibit
stimulus.body: This is a made-up example. A class makes a small exhibit about the made-up town of Nolbe. Panel 1 has a photo of an old stone well. The class needs to write a credit under the photo.

questions.question: Which line is the best credit for the photo?

options.feedback: Yes. A credit says who made the source, when, and where it is kept. Then others can check it.

options.text: Every person in Nolbe used this well
options.feedback: Not quite. This is a claim about the past, and the photo cannot prove it. A credit says who made the source. Look back at Lesson 12.

options.text: This is the best photo in our exhibit
options.feedback: Not quite. This is an opinion. A credit names who made the source and where it is kept. Look back at Lesson 12.

questions.question: Your two sources do not show what local people thought. What should you do in your exhibit?

options.text: Make up what local people said
options.feedback: Not quite. A fair exhibit does not invent evidence. Look back at Lesson 12.

options.text: Leave the gap out, so it looks complete
options.feedback: Not quite. Hiding a gap makes the story look more certain than it is. Look back at Lesson 12.

options.text: Say that this perspective is missing
options.feedback: Yes. A fair account can say, "This source does not tell us." Then visitors know what is still unsure.

results.high: Well done. You know how places, records and exhibits can tell a history fairly.
results.middle: Good work. You got many questions right. Look back at the lessons for the ones you missed, and try again if you like.
results.low: Thank you for trying. Look back at Lessons 10–12, then try again. You can take as long as you need.
